title_en: 3 killed and 1 wounded in shooting at Ohio baby shower, police say
content_en:
One of the suspected shooters was taken into custody but he was not immediately charged. A second suspected shooter was one of those killed.
In an image taken from video, police respond to the scene of a shooting in Parma, Ohio at the weekend. Photo: WEWS / NEWS 5 via AP
Three people were killed and one was injured at an Ohio baby shower during an apparent domestic dispute, authorities said.
Officers responded to a shooting on Saturday evening at Pandora’s Magical Events Venue in Parma, about 16km (10 miles) south of Cleveland, a police news release said.
Authorities said one of the suspected shooters, a 29-year-old man, was taken into custody but he was not immediately charged. Detectives were trying to determine whether the man was the aggressor or acting in self-defence, police spokesman Scott Traxler said. A second suspected shooter, a 19-year-old man, was one of the people killed, police said.
Officials have identified two of the victims as 17-year-old Leasia England and 45-year-old Jayson Townsend. Police said Townsend was the father of the woman for whom the baby shower was being held; she was not injured.
Officials have not released the names of the 19-year-old suspected shooter who was killed, or a 39-year-old woman who was shot in the leg.
Preliminary information indicates that the 19-year-old man was the father of the unborn baby and witnesses told police that he was not invited to the shower, Traxler said. The man in custody appears to be a relative of the expectant mother.
Both firearms involved in the shooting were recovered by police, officials said. Detectives were reviewing surveillance video and witnesses’ statements on Sunday to determine what led to the violent confrontation, Traxler said. Ballistics testing might be required to determine which gun shot each victim.
Prosecutors will eventually determine whether the man in custody should be charged with a crime, officials said.
By Associated Press

title_en: Russian strikes kill 6 in Kyiv region, Ukraine says
content_en:
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called Sunday’s attack part of ‘Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine’.
Emergency workers lead away a woman in distress from the site of a block of flats that partially collapsed after it was hit during a night of Russian missile and drone attacks, in Dymer, Kyiv region, Ukraine on Sunday. Photo: Reuters
Russian strikes across the Kyiv region, including on a block of flats that partially collapsed, killed at least six people, Ukraine said on Sunday, warning there could be more victims under the rubble.
Russia has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly aerial barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter of the near-five-year invasion.
An overnight strike on Dymer, around 45km (30 miles) north of the capital, hit a five-storey building.
Agence France-Presse images showed rescuers combing through the mound of smouldering rubble.
“The bodies of three victims have been recovered from the rubble,” Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said on Telegram, adding that the dead included “a woman born in 1978 and a teenager born in 2008”.
On Sunday evening, rescuers managed to pull out a child alive, Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
State Emergency Service earlier said they were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.
Residents watch as firefighters work at the site of a Russian drone strike on a shopping centre in the town of Vyshneve, Kyiv Region, Ukraine on Sunday. Photo: Reuters
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack part of “Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine”.
“The world must stop looking away. Condemn this terror, hold Russia accountable, and act now to stop the killing of innocent Ukrainians,” he said on social media.
Two other people were killed and eight wounded in Vyshneve when a Russian strike hit a supermarket.
“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.
One more person was killed when a strike set a private home ablaze in Bila Tserkva, he added.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine’s Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.
Moscow has ramped up strikes on Ukraine – particularly on its energy network – as temperatures begin to drop to around freezing.
Earlier this week, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed a “painful” response to Ukrainian strikes that damaged the Crimean bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over the annexed region.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Major Cop meetings that ended in failure, deadlock or disappointment
content_en:
The collapse of Sunday’s Cop31 talks in Turkey is just the latest setback for major United Nations environmental summits.
Cop31 President Murat Kurum gestures after officially closing the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey on Sunday. Photo: Reuters
The failure of Cop31 climate talks in Antalya is the latest in a string of disappointments at major United Nations environmental summits since the first Conference of the Parties, or Cop, in 1995.
Various previous summits have descended into acrimony or even failed completely over a lack of consensus.
2000: Cop6, The Hague
Cop6 talks in The Hague in 2000 saw talks suspended altogether before resuming months later in Bonn, the headquarters of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
That year’s event came amid disputes over a razor-thin US presidential election, with negotiators uncertain if the next leader of the largest economy would be George W Bush, a climate sceptic, or Al Gore, who later shared a Nobel Peace Prize for his climate activism.
Paradoxically, the victory of Bush – who soon repudiated the 1997 Kyoto Protocol – spurred other countries to push ahead with implementation plans when talks resumed in Bonn.
But former French chief negotiator Paul Watkinson rued an event which ended in “chaos”.
2009: Cop15, Copenhagen
Expectations were high after the election of US President Barack Obama, but Cop15 failed to deliver the binding global climate treaty many had hoped for.
Deep divisions between developed and developing countries, particularly between Washington and Beijing, prevented agreement on mandatory emissions cuts.
The conference ultimately agreed only to “take note” of the non-binding Copenhagen Accord, which included a goal of limiting warming to below 2 degrees Celsius (35.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and a pledge by wealthy countries to mobilise US$100 billion a year in climate finance by 2020.
Al Gore (right) at the Cop25 Climate Conference in Madrid, Spain in December 2019 when Gore was vice-president of the United States. Photo: NurPhoto via Getty Images
2012: Cop18, Doha
Governments agreed a second commitment period under the Kyoto Protocol but without participation from major emitters including the United States, Russia and Canada.
Critics said the deal lacked sufficient ambition and covered only a shrinking share of global emissions.
2019: Cop25, Madrid
Talks in Madrid ran more than 40 hours over schedule – the same as in Antalya this year.
Countries at Cop25 failed to agree rules governing international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
The final text disappointed vulnerable countries and environmental groups because it contained no significant increase in emissions-cutting commitments.
2022: Cop27, Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt
Nations agreed to establish a landmark “loss and damage” fund for climate-vulnerable countries.
But negotiators failed to strengthen commitments on phasing down fossil fuels amid criticism by many governments and campaigners who saw inadequate progress on commitments for cutting emissions.
2024: Cop29, Baku, Azerbaijan
Talks went into overtime amid sharp disputes over climate finance for developing countries.
Negotiators struggled to bridge divisions between wealthy and poorer nations over the scale of financial commitments.
The meeting ultimately reached a deal, avoiding outright failure, but many developing countries criticised the outcome as insufficient.
2024: Cop16 biodiversity conference, Cali, Colombia
Talks stretched into an extra night and the Colombian presidency was unable to establish a quorum, with many delegates either asleep or having already boarded return flights.
No agreement was reached on financing measures needed to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030. Discussions resumed in Rome in February 2025.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Hong Kong Election Committee race: ‘healthy’ contest with some upsets
content_en:
Nearly 99 per cent of voters cast ballots in open contests, with Ceajer Chan and Roden Tong among losers as former officials win seats.
Elected candidates in the industrial (first) subsector celebrate. Photo: Sam Tsang
Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll on Sunday drew a record turnout of nearly 99 per cent and delivered surprise upsets, with prominent business and professional leaders losing out in tighter races for seats on the body that will choose the city’s next leader.
With Beijing urging that turnout be “the higher the better”, 5,640 registered voters cast ballots on Sunday as 856 candidates competed for 723 seats on the powerful electoral college. Just 69 electors failed to vote. Overall turnout jumped by about 9 percentage points, from 89.77 per cent in 2021 to 98.79 per cent.
With no “blessing list” in most subsectors and candidates competing in a free contest, some results dealt a blow to industry heavyweights.
Former secretary for financial services and the treasury Ceajer Chan Ka-keung, now chairman of WeLab Bank, narrowly lost his re-election bid in the finance subsector by two votes. Law Society of Hong Kong president Roden Tong Man-lung was the only candidate to lose in the legal subsector, where 16 people contested 15 seats.
Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce CEO Patrick Yeung Wai-tim also failed to secure a seat in the commercial (first) subsector, which represents the chamber.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the election demonstrated “healthy competition” and highlighted the positivity of democratic development under the principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong”.
“I thank voters in the various subsectors for actively casting their votes and electing the best among the best as their preferred patriots in the Election Committee, thereby supporting Hong Kong’s future development and reforms, including the implementation of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan,” he said.
Counting started after polling stations closed at 6pm Photo: Sam Tsang
Prominent newcomers elected included former justice secretary Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, who won a seat in the legal subsector, and ex-health minister Sophia Chan Siu-chee, who was elected in the medical and health services subsector.
Former innovation and technology secretary Alfred Sit Wing-hang also won in the engineering subsector.
Other new faces included leading bankers, such as Citi Hong Kong CEO and head of banking Aveline San Pau-len and Standard Chartered Bank’s CEO for Hong Kong, Greater China and North Asia, Mary Huen Wai-yi.
Business moguls returning to the committee included Henderson Land Development chairman Martin Lee Ka-shing, Pacific Century Group chairman Richard Li Tzar-kai and Sino Land chairman Daryl Ng Win-kong.
Those elected will join 259 members returned unopposed, 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies to form the full electoral college. Their first task will be to nominate and vote in next year’s chief executive election.
Among the committee’s 40 subsectors, local representatives in the National People’s Congress and Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference accounted for 190 ex officio members, forming the largest bloc in the body.
They were followed by Hong Kong representatives in national organisations, with 110 elected members returned unopposed.
When polls opened at 9am, electors flocked to voting stations early, forming queues outside before footfall eased later in the day.
Among those who voted were CK Hutchison chairman Victor Li Tzar-kuoi, New World Development chairman Henry Cheng Kar-shun and Shun Tak Holdings executive chairwoman and managing director Pansy Ho Chiu-king.
Of the 31 contested subsectors, 14 achieved a 100 per cent turnout rate, including commercial (first) and (third), industrial (first) and (second), hotel, and import and export.
Ballot boxes are brought in for the count Photo: Sam Tsang
Full turnout was also recorded across some professional subsectors, including accountancy, engineering, legal, technology and innovation, and architectural, surveying, planning and landscape.
In 2021, only three subsectors posted a 100 per cent turnout.
The insurance subsector had the lowest turnout at 89.77 per cent, the only one below 90 per cent, and down from 93.18 per cent in 2021.
Only a small circle of 5,700 electors was eligible to vote, including government-appointed district representatives, corporate bodies named by the authorities and government-subsidised NGOs.
Electoral Affairs Commission chairman Justice David Lok Kai-hong described the turnout as “inspiring”.
“The turnout rate proves Hong Kong’s electoral system is maturing, which we are pleased to see,” he said.
Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said the record turnout suggested a greater willingness among the city’s elite to participate in politics, from running for election to voting.
“Many elites hadn’t wanted to participate in politics as they thought there would be a price to pay for political struggles,” Lau said.
“Now that there are no attacks from the opposition and less political struggle, they can see they can make more practical contributions.”
He added that the turnout and having more well-known figures running for election demonstrated a clear blueprint for political participation, where those in the patriotic camp would be able to progress and reap the rewards if they put in the effort in their respective roles.
As for the surprise results where incumbents were unseated, Lau said this was a reflection of a “free fight”, with no guarantee of winning, regardless of a candidate’s background or powerful endorsements.
“Winners also have to be vigilant. They have to do well as it is possible to be unseated in the next term,” Lau said.
While the chief executive has not divulged whether he will seek another term as city leader, several business and political heavyweights who retained their seats on the committee lauded his performance.
Lan Kwai Fong Group chairman Allan Zeman, who was re-elected in the catering subsector, backed Lee for a second term.
“If you have an idea, he won’t say ‘no’ right away. [He will say] ‘Let’s think about it’,” Zeman said, describing Lee as approachable and results-oriented.
“He has done a very good job. And speaking to other businesspeople, they all agree he is one of the best we have had.”
Counting under way at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. Photo: Sam Tsang
Chan Wing-kee, a former Standing Committee member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and an elected member in the industrial (second) subsector, described Lee as “very competent” and expressed satisfaction with his work.
But he stopped short of endorsing Lee for a second term.
“Let’s see how things develop … Hong Kong has many capable people, so whoever becomes the next chief executive, I will vote for the one with the strongest ability,” he said. “I will choose the most capable candidate.”
Bernard Chan, an ex officio member representing the social welfare subsector and head of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board, said geopolitical tensions and technological shifts remained the primary challenges to the economy and people’s livelihoods.
“I believe anyone taking up public office in the future will face major challenges they may never have encountered before,” Chan said.
“These challenges will keep coming. They are not short-term challenges, including geopolitics and new technologies that upend our economic model.”
Five polling stations operated from 9am to 6pm, but most voters turned out in the morning as they received reminders to vote early.
In the first hour of voting, turnout hit 44.74 per cent, more than triple the 14.73 per cent recorded during the same period in 2021. The overall turnout from five years ago was surpassed by 1pm.
Electoral authorities set up seating areas because of the queues to vote, with some electors saying the process took up to half an hour.
Emperor Group vice-chairman Alex Yeung Ching-loong said the long queue prompted him to leave temporarily, but added that the overall arrangement remained smooth.
Additional reporting by Jess Ma
By Matthew Cheng, Leopold Chen

title_en: Trump sees difficulties ahead if Chuck Schumer leads Senate
content_en:
The US president said working with Senate Minority Leader Schumer will be difficult once Democrats take control of Congress next year.
US President Donald Trump. Photo: Reuters
US President Donald Trump said on ⁠Sunday that it would be difficult for him to work with Senator Chuck Schumer if the Democrat is elected Senate majority leader.
“It is going to be very hard for me to ‌work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
Schumer, a New York Democrat, is currently minority leader in the Senate but Democrats ⁠next year will take control of both chambers of Congress after sweeping wins ‌in midterm elections earlier this month.
Despite the midterm wins, Schumer faces dissatisfied progressives who say a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment ‌lawmakers needs new leadership.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is making ⁠a bid for the ⁠Senate leadership, although Schumer has said he has the votes to continue as leader. A ‌closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for next month.
After the elections, Trump appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller to run ‌the ‌White House, suggesting the president will take an even more confrontational approach ‌in his last two years in office.
But Trump also has hinted he ⁠might work with Democrats on issues such as healthcare.
Speaking on CNN on Sunday, ⁠Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, said she supported expanding Medicare to cover all Americans.
“If we have to call it TrumpCare in order to ‌get it across ‌the finish line, that’s fine by me,” she said.
Flanagan said she would support Van Hollen for majority leader. “What we heard from voters is that they were pushing back against the status quo,” Flanagan said.

title_en: Israel investigates West Bank fires blamed on Israeli settlers
content_en:
Gadi Eisenkot, the rival of caretaker PM Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned the acts as ‘Jewish terrorism’ that undermine ‘regional stability’.
Palestinian men inspect burnt-out cars following a reported arson attack by Israeli settlers, in Kafr Malik, near the city of Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday. Photo: AFP
Israeli authorities said on Sunday that they opened an investigation after Palestinian cars and properties were torched in four occupied West Bank villages, in attacks a local activist said were carried out by Israeli settlers.
Israeli soldiers and police were deployed to Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani following reports and images showing vehicles set on fire and graffitied in the area, the army said, adding that it “strongly condemns” these acts.
Social media posts show vehicles in flames as well as slogans written on walls, including: “In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again,” using a biblical name for the West Bank.
“Settlers attacked the northern area on the outskirts of the village at around two in the morning,” Jihad al-Qaq, an activist from Kafr Malik village in the Ramallah governorate, told Agence France-Presse.
“They set fire to around eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans on the walls of houses.”
Israeli police said an investigation had been opened.
Gadi Eisenkot, who is involved in negotiations to form a government and is the rival of caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned these acts on social media, describing them as “Jewish terrorism” that undermines “regional stability”.
Outgoing far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir hit back, saying Eisenkot had “no idea about the facts or the investigation”.
He accused him of “selling out Israel’s security in exchange for a seat”, as Eisenkot’s bloc remains divided over whether to build a coalition through a rapprochement with Arab parties to reach a majority in parliament.
A Palestinian man points towards Hebrew graffiti sprayed on a wall of a home, following an attack reportedly carried out by Israeli settlers in Deir Abu Mashaal, near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday. Photo: AFP
Youssef Jabareen, head of the Arab-majority Joint List, described the settlers behind the attacks as the “armed wing” of far-right parties, including Ben Gvir’s.
“Settler terrorism … is a direct consequence of the deepening occupation and the policies of the Netanyahu government,” he said.
Violence in the West Bank, occupied by Israel since 1967, has surged since Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law, alongside around three million Palestinians.
Since October 2023, at least 1,119 Palestinians there have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry.
Over the same period, at least 51 Israelis, including soldiers, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during clashes in the West Bank, according to official Israeli figures.
The latest attacks come a few days after the announcement by the United Kingdom, followed by Australia, of sanctions on eight Israeli companies involved in settlement activity in the West Bank.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Has AI solved the Riemann hypothesis? Claim makes waves at 200th birthday event in China
content_en:
Chinese Fields medallist hails ‘new era’ after mathematician claims that AI solved 167-year-old problem from Bernhard Riemann.
Shing-Tung Yau, director of the Yau Mathematical Sciences Centre at Tsinghua University and chair of the bicentennial conference’s scientific committee, says he learned of the feat at the event. Photo: Nanjing Centre for Applied Mathematics
A US-based mathematician has stunned the community by claiming to have solved the nearly 170-year-old Riemann hypothesis using artificial intelligence (AI).
The news broke on Friday as a major conference opened in southern China’s Shenzhen, where world-leading mathematicians have gathered until Monday to mark the 200th anniversary of the birth of Bernhard Riemann – the German pioneer behind one of the field’s greatest unsolved problems.
The claim sent shock waves through the mathematics community, with one attending scholar saying that he was 98 per cent certain the proof was correct.
[embedded media]
Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, director of the Yau Mathematical Sciences Centre at Tsinghua University and chair of the conference’s scientific committee, told The Beijing News that he was at the event when he learned of the feat.
He said the announcement indicated that mathematics “has entered a new era,” the paper reported on Sunday.
Yau said several scholars at the conference had studied the Riemann hypothesis, including speaker and fellow Fields medallist James Maynard.
Maynard, an Oxford University professor who has made important contributions to the hypothesis, told the New York Times soon after the announcement that he believed the AI proof was likely to be correct. “I’d be 98 or 99 per cent certain,” he was quoted as saying.
The proof was unveiled on Friday by Levent Alpoge, a Turkish-American mathematician at Anthropic. He said on his personal website that he had solved the problem using the American company’s AI model, Claude.
Independent mathematicians immediately began running checks on the Lean-based code – generated by Claude over a period of six weeks – with some now confirming its mathematical accuracy.
Despite the early nod from peers, translating the solution’s underlying logic into a human-readable paper – and securing formal recognition – could take some time.
Bernhard Riemann (1826-1866) introduced his hypothesis in 1859. Photo: Handout
Riemann, born in September 1826, first proposed the hypothesis in 1859. Formally unproven for 167 years, it is widely regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
The problem is tied to the distribution of prime numbers and forms a cornerstone of modern number theory. Even without formal proof, mathematicians have long assumed the hypothesis to be true, relying on it to derive countless other theorems.
Alpoge did not publish a full readable manuscript, but rather released around 17 million lines of code written in Lean, an open-source programming language and interactive theorem prover.
“It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop’, I decided to only present Lean,” Alpoge said in a note posted on Friday alongside the code.
Terence Tao, Fields medallist and mathematician at the University of California, Los Angeles, responded in a blog post the same day.
“I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task,” Tao wrote.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems proposed in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute, with each solution carrying a US$1 million prize. Only one has been officially resolved so far.
Last month, another AI milestone took the mathematics community by storm when OpenAI published hundreds of manuscripts covering a wide range of problems – including others also on the Millennium list.
According to Yau, the use of AI could shift mathematics towards a mode of research more often used in fields like biology, physics and chemistry, where the result or answer is found first and carefully examined afterwards, rather than the step-by-step approach traditionally used by mathematicians.
“As for human intelligence, I think machines still cannot compare,” Yau told The Beijing News, while adding that the problem-solving ability of machines was still stronger than their ability to pose questions.
Levent Alpoge has released around 17 million lines of code written in Lean in support of his claim. Photo: Handout
Alpoge echoed the sentiment in his Friday note.
“This puts us in the rather extraordinary situation this age has made possible, in which I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics,” he said.
The timing has triggered speculation, given that the Riemann proof was released right after Anthropic’s initial public offering on the Nasdaq.
Alpoge addressed the issue in his note, describing the timing as “horrible” but maintaining that he would have finished earlier if he could have.
“There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false, and I am pleased that I am in circumstances where it is obviously false.”
By Victoria Bela

title_en: Yalta 2.0? Shenzhen summit was about making world less dangerous
content_en:
Nuclear risk reduction is where a three-country dialogue has the clearest rationale.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (left), Chinese President Xi Jinping (centre) and US President Donald Trump attend a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen on November 19. Photo: Sputnik/Pool via Reuters
Yalta is an easy reference point for the meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen. The gathering of the leaders of three major powers to discuss international peace and security naturally evokes earlier moments of great-power diplomacy. The four-point declaration they issued on November 19, however, points towards a different undertaking: finding enough common ground to contain the dangers of competition.
At Yalta in February 1945, wartime allies anticipated victory and negotiated arrangements for the world that would follow. Their decisions concerned Germany, Poland, Soviet entry into the war against Japan and the emerging United Nations. China has particular reason to remember that negotiations among powerful states can compromise the interests of absent countries: the agreements included Soviet privileges in Manchuria. In contrast to the Yalta Conference, Shenzhen brought together competitors without a common victory to consolidate or a shared post-war settlement to enforce.
The declaration reflects that setting. Its commitments concern UN reform, supply of refined petroleum products, state officials’ immunities and dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. It sets out no territorial settlement, security guarantees or division of the world into exclusive spheres. The breadth of its subjects contrasts with the limited detail on implementation. What emerged was an initial agenda for cooperation among governments whose interests overlap in particular areas.
The paragraph on the International Criminal Court deserves particular attention. By stressing state consent and official immunities, the three governments express a shared concern about the reach of international jurisdiction. It is the clearest sign of convergence on questions of international authority.
Activists gather outside the International Criminal Court in The Hague on November 11. The organisations Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide and Democracy for the Arab World Now have submitted evidence to the ICC seeking to establish that US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are complicit in what the organisations describe as genocide committed by Israel in the Gaza Strip. Photo: EPA
For Beijing, strategic stability offers a stronger organising principle than a new global hierarchy. In his remarks at the summit, Xi called for safeguarding the post-war international order and establishing crisis communication and prevention mechanisms. These priorities are fitting, given China’s interest in making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining its partnership with Moscow. A stable external environment supports development; a division into rival spheres could instead disrupt the economic connections on which that development depends.
Strategic stability also requires recognising the limits of influence. A durable settlement in Ukraine requires Kyiv’s participation and acceptance. European governments have decisions to make about sanctions, financing and security commitments. As European Council president Antonio Costa argued on November 13, Ukraine will decide matters concerning its territory, while Europe has a central role in Ukraine’s reconstruction and relations with the European Union. Their involvement would give any understanding reached among the three powers a stronger foundation for implementation and wider political support.
In Asia, cooperation among the three powers can build on the region’s own approaches to stability. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ Indo-Pacific outlook emphasises inclusiveness and engagement with a wide range of partners. Closer coordination among China, Russia and the US could support these efforts, taking account of regional countries’ priorities and complementing the partnerships they have developed over time.
The three countries can give fresh momentum to UN reform by developing proposals that command wider support. Charter amendments require a two-thirds vote in the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of member states, including all five permanent members of the Security Council. Their coordination can help build that consensus and strengthen the United Nations’ ability to address global challenges, with the broader membership helping to shape the outcome.
Nuclear risk reduction is where a three-country dialogue has the clearest rationale. The leaders reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, a principle all five recognised nuclear-weapon states affirmed in 2022. Its renewal matters after New Start expired in February, removing the last treaty limits on strategic nuclear arsenals deployed by the United States and Russia. The next step should be sustained work on preventing escalation and restoring predictability.
A screengrab from a video shows a Russian serviceman carrying what is said to be Russia’s nuclear briefcase as the Apec summit is held in Shenzhen on November 18. Photo: RURTR via Reuters
That work should accommodate different responsibilities. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s latest assessment shows that American and Russian nuclear stockpiles remain far larger than China’s. Washington and Moscow should pursue verifiable limits on their arsenals, while all three discuss crisis management. Making every form of risk reduction conditional on a single comprehensive arms control bargain would squander the opening Shenzhen provides.
Officials could begin by agreeing who communicates during a crisis, how urgent messages are authenticated and how dangerous military activity is clarified. Channels should be tested regularly and remain available when political relations deteriorate, precisely when misunderstandings are most dangerous and leaders most need reliable information. Human control over nuclear decisions deserves attention too. China and the US affirmed this principle in 2024; bringing Russia into a practical discussion would build on that foundation. These would be useful ways to implement the dialogue commitment.
The pledge on refined petroleum products offers another test: whether coordination can translate into reliable supplies that benefit importing countries. Regular official meetings, clear responsibilities and visible follow-through would give the declaration substance beyond a summit photograph.
Shenzhen’s contribution should be measured by whether it makes great-power competition less dangerous. China, Russia and the US have strong reasons to cooperate on that task. Their responsibility to prevent catastrophe is considerable. The wider world’s right to shape its own future remains equally fundamental.
By Sun Chenghao

But I think Asean is an example of something that almost has a G-minus architecture, because Asean has spent the last six decades trying to get 10 – now 11 – very different nations to work with one another, without there being a leader that tells everybody what to do.
The RCEP (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership) is a good example of Asean success in trade. Many out there think of RCEP as a China-led grouping – it is not. It is an Asean-initiated grouping that happens to include China; it also happens to include Japan and South Korea.

It is Asean’s ability to act in a way that fosters and encourages collaborative behaviour, without relying on a leader telling everybody else what to do, that has made RCEP a success.
[embedded media]
But if tensions heighten, could Asean be forced to pick sides? For instance, is the region re-examining its supply chains and Chinese ties because of Washington’s scrutiny of transshipments?
What Asean has done is allow its member states to navigate this rivalry without choosing sides. It has an architecture that encourages engagement with both great powers, while minimising the strategic vulnerability associated with them.
America’s official policy is that its large trade deficit with China is harmful, and it has taken to levying tariffs on imports from China and taking action against third countries for transshipment or chain-washing. A knee-jerk reaction is to assume that you must pick a side: choosing America by helping to contain China’s rise and not doing business with China, or picking China by paying no attention to America’s tariffs because you think China is the winning side.

On the America front, the tensions are between America’s consumers – who want to have cheap, high-quality Chinese goods in greater quantity – and the parts of America’s industry that compete directly with Chinese industry and want to have less competition. [embedded media]

The traditional Republican position says that America needs to be number one in the world and right now, they feel that American strength is being challenged – it doesn’t matter to them that this alternative hegemon happens to be China. On the other hand, the Democrats feel an awkwardness with China because they continue to have a vision of China as being a communist country that is authoritarian and disrespects human rights.

This group is part of industry, but they see cheap and high-quality Chinese products as good because they use them as inputs. They are quite pleased at China’s manufacturing prowess, and they don’t think of it as overcapacity or a China shock.
I have much less sympathy for tycoons whose business is now being undermined by cheap imports. If you have been undermined by a competitor, you need to figure out what to do next to win back the market

To be very clear, there are also Asean voices talking about the China shock – Indonesian industry, for instance. I am politically and socially very sympathetic with those in societies that need help. But I have much less sympathy for tycoons whose business is now being undermined by cheap imports.
If you have been undermined by a competitor, you need to figure out what to do next to win back the market. In economics, we think of this as creative destruction. These are the forces of market competition. You cannot just sit on what you are currently doing and complain about China taking away your business.

In an earlier time, it was Japan that was Asia’s champion in advancing technology. What Japan did was that it later moved on to higher value industries and it kept moving on. This created space in the industries it had left behind, with technology available for the rest of Asia to leverage. That was how a lot of the rest of Asia built out our jobs. If Chinese technology does not continue to advance and move up the value chain to create space, there will be problems.

A lot of the American rhetoric against China now resembles American rhetoric against Japan then, but the circumstances are very different.
China is much larger than Japan. On the geopolitical front, Japan had its entire military defence outsourced to the United States, which had been the case since the end of World War II. China is in a very different position, and its military defence capabilities in some dimensions are comparable to those of the United States. China will never agree to the kind of currency recalibration that Japan did.
I don’t see a clean resolution to the economic challenges that the US and China face. They are now stuck in a prisoner’s dilemma-type situation, where America will continue to draw on investment sanctions, export controls, import quotas, tariffs – many different ways to directly or indirectly disrupt the flow of Chinese goods to the US.

If the stand-off continues, the great fear is that the world would go into a Smoot-Hawley type situation, and it becomes an arms race in tariffs – which first occurred in 1930s America at the start of the Great Depression. Thankfully, that has not featured since “Liberation Day”. Countries have taken different approaches to this.

It has agreed to many things that America wanted, to a point where there was actually domestic popular pushback against what had been agreed by the political leaders in Malaysia. China is actively promoting yuan usage across Asean countries through trade settlements, panda bonds and cross-border payment systems, with Singapore serving as a top offshore yuan hub in the region. The recalibration of the Japanese yen also reflected how America controlled the international financial system. But America can lose that power of control over the world’s economy, even with the US dollar still being the world reserve currency.
So the right question could be: Can the rest of the world, for its own self-protection – not because it is trying to replace the American dollar – build enough structure so that it is no longer so vulnerable? This is what we’re seeing with the yuan in Southeast Asia. The ventures are implicitly attempts to build alternatives, not replacements, that will give all of us greater control over our financial business instead of ceding entirely to the United States.
Currency is one part of the problem. The other part is the pipes through which that currency flows. There is a Brics-plus counterpart to Swift emerging and China has the alternative CIPS, which is also a clearance and settlement system. There is mBridge and Project Nexus, which are more Southeast Asia-centred. They are multilateral and involve China, but they are not controlled by China.
I think for many Southeast Asian countries, this is a way to leapfrog the building of the international financial system, so we are keen to join in on these. We went from using currency – bypassing credit cards to a great degree – immediately into fintech and digital payment systems.
And for China, if its trade with Asean continues to grow – and it looks like it will – there is every reason to use the local currencies rather than go through the intermediary of the US dollar.

During his visit to the US in September, Xi asserted that the Thucydides Trap can be overcome. Is this possible? What does an economic relationship of managed competition without escalating to confrontation look like in practice?
I am torn on this. I want to believe that as long as we are trading, no matter other disagreements, we would feel compelled to keep this economic relationship going and build institutions and norms that help us cooperate. But I also believe that trade can create tensions, such as the China shock.
Graham Allison, who coined the term Thucydides Trap, told me that America will not be happy until it is surrounded only by friends and fish. That is because America is a large enough place; it can actually contemplate economic isolationism. But for the rest of us – especially small states like the member states of Asean – we cannot. So for us, trade is central and existential.
But for America and China, trade need not be. China’s growth trajectory was one that relied on exporting to the rest of the world, but China too is a continent-sized nation. Continent-sized nations can imagine being isolated from the rest of the world. I think the world will be poorer for it, but those two great powers can imagine that.
That is why we need to advance the G-minus agenda urgently. Because if those two great powers cannot reconcile these issues and they are forced into choosing isolationism, the rest of us – that’s 80 per cent of the world – have to figure out how to manage this.
What role, then, does Asean play in great power rivalry?
For a while, it looked like the great powers viewed great power rivalry as imposing a choice that Asean needed to take sides. Asean has been very clear it will not.
What Asean is doing now is trying to expand optionality by economically integrating with China’s supply chain, and improving its own economic strength and resilience by adding value in that supply chain. We are telling America that we respect its right to impose sanctions because it has concerns. While respecting those rights, we are able to adapt in a way that keeps us on the right side of your sanctions. We are economically resilient.
Asean is trying to work with both great powers and increase its range of options, but keep from being vulnerable to either one. I think implicit in your question is: what happens if the great power rivals then act in a way that shrinks Asean’s options? This is like the ISEAS questionnaire, which asked if forced to choose a side, which side would you choose? For the past few years, the margins have been tight.
And if we get to that point, that would mean the world would have already shrunk its optionality in ways that western Europe does not figure. Africa, Latin America and the rest of Asia does not figure for Southeast Asia any more. It would mean that everything has just merged into a background and it is only America and China left.
If we come to that point, we have lots of other things to worry about. So, we need to make sure that all of the world continues to play a role in Asean’s economic landscape. We cannot allow the great powers to shrink our optionality.

They are now stuck in a prisoner’s dilemma-type situation, where America will continue to draw on investment sanctions, export controls, import quotas, tariffs – many different ways to directly or indirectly disrupt the flow of Chinese goods to the US.
China, in turn, has now found the critical minerals and rare earths card to be a reliable way in which it practises economic statecraft. It has used that against Japan, and it could also potentially use that against the United States.
If the stand-off continues, the great fear is that the world would go into a Smoot-Hawley type situation, and it becomes an arms race in tariffs – which first occurred in 1930s America at the start of the Great Depression. Thankfully, that has not featured since “Liberation Day”. Countries have taken different approaches to this.
[embedded media]
Malaysia has done a lot of acquiescence. It has agreed to many things that America wanted, to a point where there was actually domestic popular pushback against what had been agreed by the political leaders in Malaysia. But nothing disastrous has emerged from that; Malaysia is now in the midst of an economic boom. The semiconductor industry and the AI data centre race have been very good for Malaysia. And now the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade is no longer binding because the US Supreme Court has struck down Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs.
The worry about the world falling into a Smoot-Hawley situation has not materialised, and perhaps the world can tolerate this for a little bit longer.
China is actively promoting yuan usage across Asean countries through trade settlements, panda bonds and cross-border payment systems, with Singapore serving as a top offshore yuan hub in the region. Why is Beijing focusing so heavily on Southeast Asia for its currency roll-out, and how successful have its yuan internationalisation goals been so far?
One natural question that comes out of this is: Is China setting up a replacement to the world reserve currency? I think that China is not, because China still has concerns about the convertibility of the yuan. It does not want its currency to float entirely freely on an open market, and it worries that its economy is not robust enough to withstand the potential destabilisation of highly volatile yuan. It also recognises that the presence of the Chinese yuan out there, while growing, is not that large at this point.
But that might not be the right question to ask. The notion of the world reserve currency being the US dollar has always featured prominently in geopolitical discussion, because it means that America has access to specific policies like financial sanctions that other nations do not. The recalibration of the Japanese yen also reflected how America controlled the international financial system. But America can lose that power of control over the world’s economy, even with the US dollar still being the world reserve currency.
So the right question could be: Can the rest of the world, for its own self-protection – not because it is trying to replace the American dollar – build enough structure so that it is no longer so vulnerable? This is what we’re seeing with the yuan in Southeast Asia. The ventures are implicitly attempts to build alternatives, not replacements, that will give all of us greater control over our financial business instead of ceding entirely to the United States.
Currency is one part of the problem. The other part is the pipes through which that currency flows. There is a Brics-plus counterpart to Swift emerging and China has the alternative CIPS, which is also a clearance and settlement system. There is mBridge and Project Nexus, which are more Southeast Asia-centred. They are multilateral and involve China, but they are not controlled by China.
I think for many Southeast Asian countries, this is a way to leapfrog the building of the international financial system, so we are keen to join in on these. We went from using currency – bypassing credit cards to a great degree – immediately into fintech and digital payment systems.
And for China, if its trade with Asean continues to grow – and it looks like it will – there is every reason to use the local currencies rather than go through the intermediary of the US dollar.
[embedded media]
During his visit to the US in September, Xi asserted that the Thucydides Trap can be overcome. Is this possible? What does an economic relationship of managed competition without escalating to confrontation look like in practice?
I am torn on this. I want to believe that as long as we are trading, no matter other disagreements, we would feel compelled to keep this economic relationship going and build institutions and norms that help us cooperate. But I also believe that trade can create tensions, such as the China shock.
Graham Allison, who coined the term Thucydides Trap, told me that America will not be happy until it is surrounded only by friends and fish. That is because America is a large enough place; it can actually contemplate economic isolationism. But for the rest of us – especially small states like the member states of Asean – we cannot. So for us, trade is central and existential.
But for America and China, trade need not be. China’s growth trajectory was one that relied on exporting to the rest of the world, but China too is a continent-sized nation. Continent-sized nations can imagine being isolated from the rest of the world. I think the world will be poorer for it, but those two great powers can imagine that.
That is why we need to advance the G-minus agenda urgently. Because if those two great powers cannot reconcile these issues and they are forced into choosing isolationism, the rest of us – that’s 80 per cent of the world – have to figure out how to manage this.
What role, then, does Asean play in great power rivalry?
For a while, it looked like the great powers viewed great power rivalry as imposing a choice that Asean needed to take sides. Asean has been very clear it will not.
What Asean is doing now is trying to expand optionality by economically integrating with China’s supply chain, and improving its own economic strength and resilience by adding value in that supply chain. We are telling America that we respect its right to impose sanctions because it has concerns. While respecting those rights, we are able to adapt in a way that keeps us on the right side of your sanctions. We are economically resilient.
Asean is trying to work with both great powers and increase its range of options, but keep from being vulnerable to either one. I think implicit in your question is: what happens if the great power rivals then act in a way that shrinks Asean’s options? This is like the ISEAS questionnaire, which asked if forced to choose a side, which side would you choose? For the past few years, the margins have been tight.
And if we get to that point, that would mean the world would have already shrunk its optionality in ways that western Europe does not figure. Africa, Latin America and the rest of Asia does not figure for Southeast Asia any more. It would mean that everything has just merged into a background and it is only America and China left.
If we come to that point, we have lots of other things to worry about. So, we need to make sure that all of the world continues to play a role in Asean’s economic landscape. We cannot allow the great powers to shrink our optionality.

title_en: Russia starts towing its ship hit by drones in Baltic, Finland says
content_en:
Finland’s military said Ukraine probably struck the cargo ship Sparta II on Saturday before the vessel drifted into Finnish waters.
The Finnish Border Guard extinguishes a fire on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday. Photo: Finnish Border Guard / Handout via Reuters
A Russian rescue vessel on Sunday began towing a Russian-owned cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea out of Finnish waters after two days of firefighting, Finland’s coastguard said.
The Finnish military has said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday ‌was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters.
The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured.
“Thermal cameras show that some containers are warm, but the vessel is stable enough for towing to begin,” Finland’s coastguard said in a statement. It said that responsibility for the rescue will transfer to Russia once the ship leaves Finnish waters.
Pictures and video released earlier by the Finnish coastguard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta ⁠II with water cannons during the night in a bid to put out the flames and cool down the containers stacked on its deck.
In a ‌rare instance of cross-border collaboration, out of the seven vessels helping to fight the fire, two were Russian, two were Estonian and the rest were Finnish.
Estonia and Finland are members of Nato and steadfast supporters of ‌Ukraine, and often at odds with Moscow on other issues. Finland shut all of its land border crossings with Russia in ⁠2023. Estonia will shut ⁠its own from December 1, for six months, on security grounds.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland ‌island, Finland’s Defence Forces have said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
“Smoke is still coming from the vessel and there is clearly still heat on board,” Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, sea safety officer and commander ‌of ‌the maritime sub-centre Helsinki for the Finnish Border Guard, told a press conference earlier on Sunday.
The Russian cargo ship Sparta II is sprayed with water as the fire continues in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday. Photo: Finnish Border Guard / Handout via Reuters
Kyiv has sent waves ‌of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s northwest coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading ⁠to fears that the war was spilling onto Nato territory.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of ⁠the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II ‌is a 121-metre (397-ft) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned ‌by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to LSEG data.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company’s website.
The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Treasury Department.
Lumilahti said one concern was the weather, with rain, sleet, and stronger winds expected on Sunday night and Monday.
By Reuters

title_en: US Democrats clinch at least 258 House seats, biggest since 1992
content_en:
Party prepares a 100-day agenda on living costs and Trump administration oversight after flipping 44 districts across the country.
Dawn arrives on Capitol Hill in Washington on November 2, a day before the US midterm elections. File photo: AP
House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.
Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in US President Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.
The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican congresswoman Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December run-off.
Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.
The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.
The Democrats’ majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.
It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.
“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” said Democratic congressman Jason Crow of Colorado, a former US Army Ranger.
[embedded media]
“There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorised from ICE,” he said at the Capitol, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “If you don’t feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don’t belong under this Capitol dome.”
The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.
Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.
The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.
Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power.
That includes plans to investigate how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. Photo: Reuters
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” said progressive New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.
The Democrat called the big numbers “a mandate for change”.
Congressman Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75 per cent of their time on affordability issues and 25 per cent on accountability.
“Everything should be tied back to the people – and how it’s affecting the people,” he said.
For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump’s financial dealings, they should connect the dots: “How does that affect people’s pocketbooks?”
[embedded media]
The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned investigations into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations – a standard oversight function of Congress – may amount to “blatant criminality”.
After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority – meaning any few Republican lawmakers could derail the agenda – the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to manoeuvre.
Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on January 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of Republican opposition.
“We’re not a monolith – people come to the caucus with different ideas – it’s OK,” said Louisiana congressman Troy Carter, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.
Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They are far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.
Congressman Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.
“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.
The Republicans’ high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.
By Associated Press

title_en: US seeks answers on Nvidia’s sale of chips to China, Bessent says
content_en:
The US treasury secretary said he will find out who was in charge of compliance at the company formerly led by Jensen Huang.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington. Photo: AFP
The US ⁠is seeking answers from Nvidia on ⁠its chip sales to China and will find out who was in charge of compliance at the company formerly led by Jensen Huang, who resigned following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, US Treasury Secretary ‌Scott Bessent said on Sunday.
“We’ve been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers … It behoves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent told the CBS programme Face the Nation.
Reports about Huang’s relationship with a ⁠woman whom US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy and his extramarital affair with a ‌company executive led to his resignation and investigations by US regulators and the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation), congressional action, an internal review and a proposed ‌investor class-action lawsuit.
Days after Huang’s resignation, US President Donald Trump’s administration issued a rule to ⁠further restrict China’s ⁠access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, tightening controls ahead of Trump’s trip to China last ‌week for talks with President Xi Jinping.
Bessent said the chipmaker’s board of directors is working to determine what had ‌happened and ‌he expressed confidence that it would “come up with some very fulsome and robust ‌answers”.
“We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there,” Bessent said. “We ⁠will see which level of the business knew about this. Was it at the lower ⁠levels? Was it at the middle level? Did it go all the way to the top?”
Trump said on Friday that he would like to ‌see Huang apologise and return ‌to Nvidia. Asked whether he agreed with Trump, Bessent said more information is needed.
“I think we have to see where the buck stops,” Bessent said.
Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones has said the board will not rehire Huang.
By Reuters

title_en: US intelligence chief says Trump’s ‘friend’ label for Putin is ‘entirely appropriate’
content_en:
Jay Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterised as a betrayal of US values after Trump met Putin and Xi for talks in China.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) and US President Donald Trump at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China on Thursday. Photo: Sputnik / Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Pool via Reuters
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday it was “entirely appropriate” for US President Donald Trump to call Russian leader Vladimir Putin his friend.
Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterised as a betrayal of American values after Trump met Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for rare three-way talks.
The summit last week in China seemed to be more symbolism than substance, but Trump and his top aides have described it as a historic gathering of the three countries with the largest nuclear arsenals.
Trump raised eyebrows with his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his “friend”, which continued on Saturday, when the Republican president posted an image on Truth Social of him shaking hands with a smiling Putin under the caption, “My Friend.”
“In that circle – in that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate,” Clayton said on ABC’s This Week.
He had a similar assessment on CNN’s State of the Union, where he said it was “historic” and “remarkable” for Trump to meet the presidents of the other leading nuclear powers.
“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.
Jay Clayton, director of US National Intelligence. Photo: Reuters
Like Trump, Clayton declined when pressed to characterise Putin as a friend of the United States, noting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, an American ally.
“He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said on ABC.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York criticised the summit as a “historic embarrassment” for the United States.
“America would have been far better off if Trump just stayed home,” Schumer said from the Senate floor.
Trump’s fondness for Putin has been a defining characteristic of Trump’s two terms as president. He beamed when meeting the Russian leader last week.
After returning to Washington, Trump made no effort in the White House briefing room on Friday to walk back the comments and he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the US.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, then immediately shifted to his “very good” personal relationship with Putin.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with)]” Trump said. “It’s actually very good.”

title_display: US intelligence chief says Trump’s ‘friend’ label for Putin is ‘entirely appropriate’
content_display:
Jay Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterised as a betrayal of US values after Trump met Putin and Xi for talks in China.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) and US President Donald Trump at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China on Thursday. Photo: Sputnik / Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Pool via Reuters
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday it was “entirely appropriate” for US President Donald Trump to call Russian leader Vladimir Putin his friend.
Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterised as a betrayal of American values after Trump met Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for rare three-way talks.
The summit last week in China seemed to be more symbolism than substance, but Trump and his top aides have described it as a historic gathering of the three countries with the largest nuclear arsenals.
Trump raised eyebrows with his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his “friend”, which continued on Saturday, when the Republican president posted an image on Truth Social of him shaking hands with a smiling Putin under the caption, “My Friend.”
“In that circle – in that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate,” Clayton said on ABC’s This Week.
He had a similar assessment on CNN’s State of the Union, where he said it was “historic” and “remarkable” for Trump to meet the presidents of the other leading nuclear powers.
“In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” Clayton said.
Jay Clayton, director of US National Intelligence. Photo: Reuters
Like Trump, Clayton declined when pressed to characterise Putin as a friend of the United States, noting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, an American ally.
“He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton said on ABC.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York criticised the summit as a “historic embarrassment” for the United States.
“America would have been far better off if Trump just stayed home,” Schumer said from the Senate floor.
Trump’s fondness for Putin has been a defining characteristic of Trump’s two terms as president. He beamed when meeting the Russian leader last week.
After returning to Washington, Trump made no effort in the White House briefing room on Friday to walk back the comments and he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the US.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said, then immediately shifted to his “very good” personal relationship with Putin.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with)]” Trump said. “It’s actually very good.”
By Associated Press
